# FM 3-25.26 Map Reading and Land Navigation (Excerpt)

This excerpt summarizes grid coordinates and major terrain features for local retrieval practice.

## Grid Coordinates

### Precision Levels

Military maps overlay numbered grid lines to define horizontal and vertical positions across an area.
Read right along the easting axis first, then read up along the northing axis.

A four-digit grid coordinate locates a point within a 1,000-meter grid square.
A six-digit grid coordinate locates a point within a 100-meter square for standard tactical navigation.
An eight-digit grid coordinate locates a point within a 10-meter square for artillery targets and landing zones.

To measure a six-digit coordinate, place the coordinate scale on the lower-left corner of the grid square.
Align the vertical edge with the easting grid line and read the tenths value from left to right.
Next, count tenths upward along the vertical scale to obtain the northing digit.
Always record an even number of digits so easting precision matches northing precision.
Verify each digit against adjacent contour lines and road intersections before transmitting coordinates over radio nets.

When operating without a plastic protractor scale, subdivide the grid square visually into tenths along both axes.
Estimate the center point at five tenths, then refine the position inward toward the nearest grid line.
Confirm the final coordinate using nearby recognizable landmarks such as road junctions, bridges, or prominent hilltops.
Check that the two-letter 100,000-meter grid zone designator precedes the numeric digits when reporting across sector boundaries.

### Plotting Back Azimuths

Convert a magnetic azimuth to a grid azimuth using the declination diagram on the map margin.
Add 180 degrees when the azimuth measures less than 180 degrees.
Subtract 180 degrees when the azimuth measures 180 degrees or greater.

## Major Terrain Features

### Hilltop and Ridge

A hilltop appears on a contour map as concentric closed contour loops around a central peak.
A ridge appears as a line of high ground with lower terrain sloping away on both sides.

### Saddle and Valley

A saddle is a dip or low point between two adjacent areas of higher ground.
A valley is a stretched-out groove in the land usually formed by a stream or river.
